conditions.name: Adult immunization and catch-up
conditions.overview: Selected adult catch-up, HPV, pregnancy Tdap and recombinant-zoster decisions from CDC professional notes. This is a preventive study topic, not an additional diagnosis.

sections.title: Interrupted adult series
sections.text: For incomplete or unknown adult vaccination histories, give recommended vaccines. Extended intervals do not require restarting a vaccine series or adding extra doses solely because of the delay.

sections.title: HPV age and prior-series boundaries
sections.text: CDC recommends completing HPV vaccination through age 26. Starting at age 15 or older uses three doses at 0, 1–2 and 6 months. For ages 27–45, vaccination is based on shared clinical decision-making, rather than automatic catch-up for every adult. A valid completed HPV series needs no additional dose. Contraindications and special situations still apply.
sections.sourceLocator: Human papillomavirus vaccination: Routine vaccination; Shared clinical decision-making

sections.title: HPV and immunocompromising conditions
sections.text: People with immunocompromising conditions, including HIV, complete a three-dose HPV series even if the series begins at ages 9–14. Age eligibility and special-situation recommendations still apply.

sections.title: Tdap in each pregnancy
sections.text: CDC specifies one Tdap dose during each pregnancy, preferably in the early part of gestational weeks 27–36. A dose in a previous pregnancy does not replace the dose for the current pregnancy.
sections.sourceLocator: Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccination: Special situations

sections.title: Recombinant zoster after previous shingles
sections.text: For adults age 50 or older, CDC specifies a two-dose recombinant-zoster series, normally 2–6 months apart, regardless of prior herpes zoster. This product does not prevent primary varicella; pregnancy and immunocompromising conditions have separate considerations.
sections.sourceLocator: Zoster vaccination: Routine vaccination; Special situations

questions.stem: A fictional 25-year-old adult has never received HPV vaccine and has no contraindication or immunocompromising condition. Which CDC age-based category applies?

choices.text: Routine/catch-up completion through age 26
Shared decision-making category for ages 27–45
No vaccination because adulthood has begun
Single-dose completion regardless of age at initiation
Repeat a previously completed series

questions.explanation: At age 25, HPV vaccination falls in routine/catch-up completion through age 26. Starting at age 15 or older uses a three-dose series.

distractorExplanations.B: The 27–45 shared-decision category does not describe this 25-year-old.
distractorExplanations.D: Initiation at age 15 or older requires three doses, not an assumed single dose.
distractorExplanations.E: The vignette describes an unvaccinated adult, not a completed series.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the HPV routine/catch-up age boundary.

questions.stem: A fictional healthy 34-year-old adult has never received HPV vaccine. Which approach matches the CDC age category?

choices.text: Automatic catch-up for every adult over age 26
Shared clinical decision-making about HPV vaccination
A blanket contraindication solely because of age 34
Use the adolescent two-dose schedule regardless of starting age
Require an additional dose for anyone with a completed valid series

questions.explanation: For adults age 27–45, HPV vaccination is based on shared clinical decision-making. If first initiated at age 34, the adult notes specify a three-dose series.

distractorExplanations.A: Automatic routine catch-up through age 26 does not extend to everyone age 34.
distractorExplanations.C: The notes provide a shared-decision category at this age, not an age-only contraindication.
distractorExplanations.D: Age at initial vaccination determines the series; starting at 34 is not the 9–14 category.
distractorExplanations.E: CDC does not recommend additional doses after a valid completed series.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish HPV shared decision-making from routine adult catch-up.

questions.stem: A fictional 20-year-old adult with HIV diagnosed before age 12 began HPV vaccination at age 12 while already immunocompromised. Two valid doses of the prescribed three-dose course have been received. Which total series length is specified by the CDC special-situation rule?

choices.text: One dose
Two doses because all age-12 initiations use two
Three doses because an immunocompromising condition is present
Annual HPV boosters indefinitely
No HPV vaccine at any age in people with HIV

questions.explanation: CDC specifies three doses with immunocompromising conditions, including HIV, even when initiation occurred at ages 9–14.

distractorExplanations.A: The immunocompromising-condition recommendation is a three-dose series.
distractorExplanations.B: The three-dose special-situation rule overrides the usual two-dose initiation category.
distractorExplanations.D: The cited notes specify a series, not indefinite annual boosters.
distractorExplanations.E: The notes explicitly address HPV vaccination in people with HIV.

questions.stem: In a fictional pregnancy vignette, a 29-year-old is at 28 weeks and received Tdap in a previous pregnancy two years ago. There is no contraindication. Which plan matches the CDC notes?

choices.text: Wait ten years from the previous dose
Omit Tdap because any previous pregnancy dose is sufficient
Give Tdap only after delivery
Give one Tdap dose in this pregnancy within the preferred 27–36-week window
Give a new three-dose primary series solely because of pregnancy

questions.explanation: CDC recommends one Tdap dose during each pregnancy, preferably early in gestational weeks 27–36. A previous pregnancy dose does not remove this recommendation.

distractorExplanations.A: The pregnancy-specific recommendation is a dose during each pregnancy.
distractorExplanations.C: This vignette is within the preferred gestational window.
distractorExplanations.E: Pregnancy alone is not the cited indication to restart a primary series.

questions.stem: A fictional immunocompetent 62-year-old has recovered from previous shingles and has never received recombinant zoster vaccine. Which CDC routine recommendation applies?

choices.text: No vaccination because prior shingles replaces vaccination
One dose because shingles counts as dose one
Live zoster vaccine is the only relevant product
Wait until age 80 solely because of prior shingles
Two recombinant-zoster doses normally 2–6 months apart

questions.explanation: CDC recommends two recombinant-zoster doses for adults age 50 or older regardless of previous herpes zoster.

distractorExplanations.A: Previous shingles does not remove the routine recommendation.
distractorExplanations.B: Prior illness is not counted as a vaccine dose in the cited recommendation.
distractorExplanations.C: The routine recommendation cited here is recombinant-zoster vaccination.
distractorExplanations.D: The age threshold in these notes is 50, not a prior-shingles rule to wait until 80.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that previous shingles does not replace recombinant-zoster vaccination.

questions.stem: A fictional adult missed the next dose of a previously started, still-indicated vaccine series by several years. Earlier doses were valid, and no product-specific exception applies. What general CDC principle governs this delay?

choices.text: Complete the indicated remaining doses without restarting solely for the extended interval
Repeat every earlier valid dose
Add an extra dose solely to compensate for elapsed time
Declare the series complete despite missing indicated doses
Stop using the documented earlier doses

questions.explanation: CDC adult notes say not to restart or add doses to a series because of extended intervals. The remaining schedule must still follow the relevant vaccine notes.

distractorExplanations.B: Extended intervals alone do not require repeating valid previous doses.
distractorExplanations.C: The notes prohibit extra doses solely because of a prolonged interval.
distractorExplanations.D: Missing indicated doses still require completion.
distractorExplanations.E: The stated prior doses are valid; their documentation remains relevant.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the adult no-restart rule without ignoring vaccine-specific exceptions.

sections.title: Delayed childhood series
sections.text: The CDC catch-up table says a vaccine series does not need restarting regardless of elapsed time between doses. Catch-up still requires checking each vaccine’s minimum age, intervals, maximum age and notes.
sections.sourceLocator: Children age 4 months through 6 years: opening no-restart statement

sections.title: Adolescent HPV series
sections.text: For immunocompetent adolescents who start HPV vaccination at ages 9–14, CDC uses two doses at 0 and 6–12 months, with at least five months between doses. Starting at age 15 or older uses three doses. Immunocompromising conditions require three doses even with younger initiation.
sections.sourceLocator: Human papillomavirus vaccination: Routine and catch-up vaccination; Special situations

sections.title: Rotavirus catch-up age limits
sections.text: Do not begin a rotavirus series on or after age 15 weeks, 0 days. The final dose cannot be given after age 8 months, 0 days. Delayed-series principles do not override these vaccine-specific maximum ages.

sections.title: MenACWY adolescent booster boundary
sections.text: CDC routine MenACWY vaccination uses doses at ages 11–12 and 16. A first catch-up dose at ages 16–18 is a one-dose catch-up schedule; a first dose at 13–15 needs a booster at 16–18, at least eight weeks later. Risk-based indications have separate schedules.
sections.sourceLocator: Meningococcal serogroup A, C, W, Y vaccination: Routine vaccination; Catch-up vaccination

sections.title: Infant hepatitis B final-dose minimum age
sections.text: For routine infant hepatitis B vaccination, the final dose has a minimum age of 24 weeks. Validating a final dose also requires checking minimum intervals, not age alone.
sections.sourceLocator: Hepatitis B vaccination: Routine vaccination; final dose and minimum intervals

sections.title: Newborn maternal hepatitis B exposure
sections.text: For a fictional newborn whose mother is HBsAg-positive, the CDC notes specify monovalent hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin in separate limbs within 12 hours of birth regardless of birth weight. Low birth weight changes the subsequent series; this section does not supply that entire pathway.
sections.sourceLocator: Hepatitis B vaccination: Mother is HBsAg-positive

questions.stem: A fictional immunocompetent 13-year-old received the first HPV dose six months ago at age 12. The dose was valid and there is no contraindication. Which series plan matches the CDC adolescent notes?

choices.text: Restart the series after the six-month interval
Give three additional doses because the learner is now 13
Give the second dose to complete the two-dose series
No second dose is needed
Change to annual boosters

questions.explanation: Starting at age 9–14 uses two doses at 0 and 6–12 months for an immunocompetent adolescent. Six months exceeds the five-month minimum.

distractorExplanations.A: This recommended interval does not trigger a restart.
distractorExplanations.B: The immunocompetent 9–14 initiation category is two total doses.
distractorExplanations.D: The cited category requires a second dose.
distractorExplanations.E: The notes specify completion of a series, not annual boosters.

questions.learningObjective: Apply HPV initiation age and minimum interval together.

questions.stem: A fictional healthy infant is 17 weeks old and has never received rotavirus vaccine. Which catch-up principle is correct?

choices.text: Start the series now because all catch-up vaccines have no maximum age
Wait until the first birthday to start
Restart a nonexistent prior series
Do not initiate because the first-dose maximum age has passed
Give the first dose anytime before age 8 months

questions.explanation: CDC says not to start rotavirus vaccination on or after 15 weeks, 0 days. The eight-month final-dose limit is not the initiation limit.

distractorExplanations.A: Rotavirus has a specific maximum initiation age.
distractorExplanations.B: Waiting until the first birthday does not satisfy the stated initiation limit.
distractorExplanations.C: The vignette describes no prior rotavirus doses.
distractorExplanations.E: The eight-month maximum concerns the final dose, not starting the series.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish rotavirus initiation and final-dose maximum ages.

questions.stem: A fictional healthy 16-year-old received MenACWY at age 11 and has no risk-based indication requiring a different schedule. Which routine plan is supported?

choices.text: No further dose because the age-11 dose completes routine adolescent vaccination
Restart the entire childhood series
Give an annual MenACWY booster indefinitely
Wait until age 25 for the routine adolescent booster
Give the routine MenACWY booster at age 16

questions.explanation: CDC routine MenACWY vaccination includes a dose at ages 11–12 and a booster at age 16.

distractorExplanations.A: The routine adolescent schedule includes the age-16 booster.
distractorExplanations.B: This is a scheduled booster, not a series restart.
distractorExplanations.C: The cited routine schedule does not require indefinite annual boosters.
distractorExplanations.D: Age 16 is the routine booster age in this vignette.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the routine adolescent MenACWY booster age.

questions.stem: A fictional healthy 17-year-old has never received MenACWY and has no risk-based indication for a different schedule. Which catch-up plan is specified for an initial dose at this age?

choices.text: One MenACWY catch-up dose
Two doses four weeks apart for every healthy 17-year-old
First dose now and routine booster at age 16
Restart a childhood series that was never started
Postpone initial catch-up until age 21

questions.explanation: CDC specifies one catch-up MenACWY dose when the first dose is at age 16–18, absent a separate risk-based indication.

distractorExplanations.B: The cited healthy age-16–18 catch-up category is one dose.
distractorExplanations.C: A future plan cannot place a booster at an age already passed.
distractorExplanations.D: No prior series exists to restart.
distractorExplanations.E: The stated catch-up category covers this adolescent now.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish initial MenACWY catch-up at 16–18 from earlier initiation.

questions.stem: In a fictional infant immunization vignette, minimum dose-to-dose intervals for hepatitis B are satisfied, but a planned final dose would be given at age 20 weeks. What additional age constraint must the learner recognize?

choices.text: Final doses have no minimum age
The final dose cannot be valid before age 24 weeks
Age 12 weeks is the final-dose minimum
Every infant must wait until age two years
The minimum age is waived solely because dose-to-dose intervals are valid

questions.explanation: The CDC infant HepB notes specify a minimum final-dose age of 24 weeks. Satisfying dose-to-dose intervals does not remove that age requirement.

distractorExplanations.A: The final dose has an explicit age minimum.
distractorExplanations.C: The cited minimum is 24 weeks, not 12.
distractorExplanations.D: The notes do not impose an age-two-years minimum.
distractorExplanations.E: Age and minimum intervals are separate requirements.

questions.learningObjective: Validate hepatitis B final-dose age independently of dose intervals.

questions.stem: A fictional newborn has a mother with a documented positive HBsAg result. Which combination and timing are specified in the CDC newborn notes, regardless of birth weight?

choices.text: Hepatitis B vaccine alone at age six months
HBIG alone after discharge
Monovalent HepB vaccine and HBIG in separate limbs within 12 hours of birth
Only maternal antiviral treatment counts as newborn prophylaxis
Wait for the first routine outpatient visit before either product

questions.explanation: The CDC notes specify monovalent HepB vaccine plus HBIG in separate limbs within 12 hours of birth for an infant of an HBsAg-positive mother. Subsequent doses depend in part on birth weight.

distractorExplanations.A: This omits immediate prophylaxis and HBIG.
distractorExplanations.B: The specified combination includes vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours.
distractorExplanations.D: The newborn recommendation still specifies both products.
distractorExplanations.E: Delaying until a later visit does not meet the stated timing.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the documented maternal-HBsAg-positive newborn prevention pathway.
